Issue zero

From the editors

Every day the Sotabosc desk reads the city: openings, festivals, workshops, the small rooms where things start. Most of it ends up on screens in cafés, studios and coworking spaces, as Sotabosc TV. This is the same desk, on paper.

Issue zero follows the rule we offer every business in our network: most of the pages for the world around you, the rest for your own house. Here the house is us. Pages 3 to 9 are Barcelona in November. Pages 10 to 15 explain what Sotabosc is, and how a café, a gallery or a studio can have a channel and a magazine of its own.

We summarise, we credit, we link out. Nobody appears without saying yes.

— The Sotabosc desk

pages.title: Lead: The city gets a screen
pages.html:
The cityThe leadDigital arts
Biennial of Digital Arts · DHub

The city gets a screen

Barcelona’s first Biennial of Digital Arts opens with forty works at DHub, and plans a screen for art in a metro hall.

Words by the Sotabosc desk

For a long time, digital art in Barcelona lived in festivals: two loud days at a fairground, then gone until next year. This week the city tried something slower. The first Biennial of Digital Arts opened at the Disseny Hub on 25 November and will run, in pieces, until March.

Its first exhibition is called “Vectors. Digital art to think about the future”. Curated by Irma Vidal i Òdena, it brings together around forty works by thirty-three artists, and it does something festivals rarely have room for: it puts the pioneers in the same room as the people they made possible.

So Vera Molnár, Elena Asins, Manfred Mohr, John Whitney and Lillian Schwartz, who were drawing with machines before most of us had seen one, hang alongside Mario Klingemann, Joana Moll, Mónica Rikić, Anna Carreras, Alba G. Corral, Hamill Industries, Playmodes and Zachary Lieberman.

The Biennial is directed by Pep Salazar and organised by the City Council, the Generalitat’s culture department and the Barcelona Creativity & Design Foundation, with money from the Ministry of Culture.

Continued on page 4 →

03Sotabosc · Barcelona Edition · No. 0

pages.title: Lead, continued
pages.html:
The cityThe city gets a screen, continuedDigital arts

The most interesting part of the Biennial may not be in a gallery at all. In the coming months a large screen for digital art will go up in the new vestibule of the Glòries metro station, the entrance that leads straight into DHub, with a twin in the building’s hall.

It will be called Pantalla DHub, and from December it will carry “Resonances. The city that resonates”, a programme curated by İrem Erkin in twelve chapters, each about a different side of the city. The names are a fair map of Barcelona’s scene: Onionlab, Domestic Data Streamers, Hamill Industries, Desilence, Six N. Five, alongside Universal Everything, Sofia Crespo and Wang & Söderström.

Art that you pass on the way to somewhere else is still art. It may be the art most people see.

That is a quiet change of address. A screen in a metro hall is not a museum wall; nobody buys a ticket, and most people are on their way somewhere else. Work made for it has to be legible in ten seconds and still worth a second look on the hundredth morning.

The rest of the programme is built to bring the public in. Zachary Lieberman opened the week with a drawing workshop at DHub. From 4 to 20 December, Domestic Data Streamers and the anthropologist and filmmaker Aída Bueno show “1.5 minutes”, a piece made from colonial photographs and generative AI. On 10 December, CREATEACH spends a day on art, AI and how we decide what to make with them.

Under a +Biennial label, the city’s own players join in: Parallel Futures, Talking Galleries at Arts Santa Mònica, Anna Carreras at La Capella, and a mapping of Casa Batlló by Joanie Lemercier and Juliette Bibasse with Maria Arnal.

In February the professionals arrive: The Shift Salon with London’s Barbican on 2 and 3 February, a symposium on 3 and 4, and Circuit on the 5th, when local studios open their doors.

Why it matters to us Screens are becoming public space

Pantalla DHub is a city doing at scale what Sotabosc TV does one room at a time: putting culture on the screens people already walk past. The difference is the room. In a metro hall you have seconds; in a café, a studio or a coworking space you have half an hour, and a screen can tell a longer story about the city outside.

pages.title: MIRA at fifteen
pages.html:
The cityFestival05
MIRA · Fira Montjuïc · 6–7 November

Eyes that look back

Fifteen editions in, Barcelona’s digital arts festival handed perception to the machines and asked what they see.

MIRA has spent fifteen years putting digital art on the same bill as contemporary music, in a city that watched the medium grow up. This year the art programme had eleven installations and performances, sharing two days with a twenty-seven act music line-up.

The theme was easy to read: post-human ecosystems, and perception handed over to machines. Pinar Yoldas showed a speculative ecology built to survive inside the Great Pacific Garbage Patch. Sarabiotic’s environment, drawn from the ocean floor, shifted as people walked past. Andreas Lutz built a system that learns from the faces it meets.

Then the body entered the interface. AEDOSSYNTH gave three artificial heads a voice; Onionlab turned the main stage into a surface of light that answered the sound.

The quieter story was the schools. Students from EINA, ELISAVA, IED Barcelona and La Salle showed work beside the headliners. Fifteen years of that has built a pipeline from Barcelona’s design schools onto the festival floor.

Five works worth knowing
Pinar YoldasAn Ecosystem of Excess: life designed for a sea of plastic
SarabioticEvolutionary Signals: an ocean-floor world that reacts to visitors
Andreas LutzA system that learns from the faces it meets
Marc Arnela, I AM JASAEDOSSYNTH: three artificial heads, one synthetic voice
OnionlabResonant Field: the main stage as a surface of light

pages.title: Briefs
pages.html:
The cityBriefsNovember

Briefs

four rooms, one month
Film · Cinemes Aribau

Eleven days of music documentaries

In-Edit’s 24th edition filled Cinemes Aribau from 29 October to 8 November with films about people who organised their lives around a sound, from Carlo Padial’s El Doble to 152 minutes on Voïvod. New this year: an award for music videos, and a screening with Arrels Fundació.

Sotabosc journal, 24 October
Talks · Hangar, Poblenou

Where does AI actually live?

Three free Thursday evenings at Hangar asked a grounded question: about training data and the books bought up to feed it, about the chips that go to data centres first, and about small models that run on a laptop or a Raspberry Pi.

Sotabosc journal, 24 October
Workshop · Hangar

Blender from zero

Desirée Quevedo’s #Blendícete teaches the free 3D suite to anyone curious enough to turn up. Volume one ran four Thursdays in November; volume two, on animation, starts 14 January at €90. Bring a laptop; the rest is taught.

Sotabosc journal, 17 October
Design · Online

A library of shapes you can take apart

Book of Shapes, by the Bremen designer Nikolaj Sokolowski, is about ninety generative patterns, from woven grids to Truchet arcs. Each one is a small chain of steps you can open, change and remake, which makes it a teacher as much as a catalogue.

Sotabosc journal, 8 October
Also closed this month A labyrinth of glass at the Barcelona Pavilion. From 12 to 22 November, Ciro Najle and Josep Ferrando laid a transparent maze over Mies van der Rohe and Lilly Reich’s travertine podium, turning the building’s famous see-through calm into something less settled. ArchDaily, 12 November

pages.title: Ideas
pages.html:
The cityIdeasMarginalia

A set of generative science pieces for a 4K wall display makes a simple promise: nothing on screen is animated. Each piece is a single HTML file that simulates something real and draws what happens. A run that goes badly is allowed to go badly, because none of it is scripted.

Four thousand starlings turn over a field at dusk with nobody leading. About 137,000 particles behave like slime mould and grow a transport network. A survey car hunts methane leaks, and the colour on the street is not the gas but the survey’s growing belief about where it is.

Others draw on real data: lightning from a weather satellite, the 4,737 nearest stars known to carry planets, artworks pulled live from the Art Institute of Chicago’s open collection. All of it is free to open and take apart.

A screen can show the world working, not just a picture of it. This is the idea behind Sotabosc TV’s interludes: art that is drawn live, so the room never sees the same minute twice. Sotabosc journal, 11 October. Pieces: WorldByJoe, tv-art-display on GitHub
Did you know A coral can be brought back by touch

A Stanford team placed bleached and healthy coral of the same genetic line in contact. Within a week, sometimes three days, the healthy partner’s symbionts crossed over and the pale one filled back with colour. It is a lab result, not a reef method yet, but it turns surviving patches into a source rather than a remnant.

Sotabosc journal, 21 October

The houseAbout Sotabosc10

The life under the canopy

sotabosc (Catalan, n.): the undergrowth. Everything that grows beneath the tall trees, where most of a forest’s life actually happens.

Barcelona’s landmarks get the attention. Sotabosc is about the rest: the galleries, workshops, studios, roasters and rooms where the city’s creative life actually grows.

379 places in the directory
94 art galleries
88 specialty coffee bars
67 places to work
31 music venues
The directory A living map Every place is a record that keeps changing: what it is, where it is, what is on there. Places decide how they appear, and nothing about them is shown without their say.
The desk Read every day Each morning we read the city’s open agenda, the journal and the culture press, and write short pieces in our own words, always credited and linked.
The city Walk into it At sotabosc.world the directory becomes a small 3D city. Fly between neighbourhoods, step inside a building, and collect a stamp in your passport for each kingdom you visit.

pages.title: The network
pages.html:
The houseThe network13

Neighbours, not noise

A café’s guests are a gallery’s next visitors. A coworking space’s members are a bookshop’s best customers. Barcelona’s small places have always sent people to each other by word of mouth; the network makes that a habit.

Every host can invite neighbours onto its screen, and appear on theirs. Only places that both say yes are paired, and only for as long as they want. Nobody buys their way onto another host’s wall.

The magazine does the same on paper: each issue has a page for the street, and the places on it are chosen by an editor, not an auction.

For visitors, the city at sotabosc.world keeps a passport. Each place they visit adds a stamp from its kingdom, which is a small reason to walk one street further.

The more hosts there are in a neighbourhood, the richer each screen becomes: more local stories, more events, more reasons for a guest to stay a little longer and come back.

A café’s guests are a gallery’s next visitors. The network just makes it a habit.

Both say yes Neighbours appear only when both places opt in.
Labelled, always Recommendations are marked as such on screen and on paper.
Leave any time A place can step out, and its content goes with it.

pages.title: Become a host
pages.html:
The houseBecome a host

From a coffee to on air

Four steps, usually inside a month. Nothing to install on your own computers, nothing to learn.

1
A conversation We visit, sit where your guests sit, and look at where a screen would belong. If it is not a fit, we say so.
2
Your taste Which parts of the city your place cares about, which neighbours you admire, how much of your own house you want on air.
3
An afternoon’s install A screen and a small computer behind it. It plays on its own, and keeps playing if the internet drops.
4
On air We tune the first week with you. After that, send photos and news from your phone and the desk does the rest.
Start the conversation sotabosc.world/contact Tell us about your place, and we’ll come and sit in it.
